title: World Models Dream of Success:Diagnosing and Repairing Failure Insensitivity in Robot World Models

paper.title: World Models Dream of Success: Diagnosing and Repairing Failure Insensitivity in Robot World Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Robot world models support policy evaluation, planning, and synthetic data generation, but these applications require predictions that distinguish successful actions from failures.
Across four released checkpoints from two architecture families, we observe weak sensitivity to action changes and success-like predictions on verified failures.
Although recent work incorporates failures into model training, which data can repair released checkpoints without changing their architecture or training objective still remains underexplored.
To this end, we introduce CureWM , which constructs alternative actions from successful demonstrations across a severity grid, verifies their outcomes through execution in simulation or on hardware, and fine-tunes released models on the resulting failures and surviving successes alongside nominal demonstrations.
This construction provides controlled action contrasts from shared starting contexts.
On 484 held-out LIBERO failure counterfactuals, optimism falls from 80% after fine-tuning on the official data to 30–43% across four independently fine-tuned CureWM models (38% mean).
In two separate evaluations on a physical robot arm, failure predictions scored as success-like by a latent-distance diagnostic decrease from 90% after fine-tuning on successful demonstrations alone to 33% with CureWM.
With failure counts per task, successful replay data, and training budget matched, counterfactual failures yield a success–failure value gap of 0.124, compared with 0.014 for freshly collected on-policy failures.
These findings support execution-verified counterfactual replay for post-hoc repair and show why reduced optimism must be evaluated alongside success–failure discrimination.
Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/CureWM .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Robot world models learn to predict how environments evolve in response to actions, from latent dynamics models to generative video simulators ( Hafner et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; NVIDIA, 2025a ) . In the robotic domain, their predictions support policy evaluation in imagination ( Guo et al., 2026 ) , action selection and planning ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , and synthetic experience generation for policy learning ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) . These applications require more than visually plausible futures: a model must distinguish actions that accomplish the task from those that fail. If failing actions receive high success values or generate success-like futures, decisions based on these predictions can favor actions that do not achieve the intended outcome. However, how to repair failure prediction in released robot world models still remains underexplored. MiraBench ( Yang et al., 2026 ) found optimism bias in action-conditioned predictions, but diagnosing such failure insensitivity does not tell us which training data could correct it. In particular, failed trajectories need not teach a model how alternative actions from the same context change the outcome. This distinction matters for released checkpoints: simply adding failures may lower predicted success across both successful and failing actions, reducing the optimism without improving discrimination. Therefore, the question is which kind of data enable post-hoc repair of action-conditioned predictions, and how to distinguish that repair from a general shift toward pessimism. Concurrent work, such as FACT ( Peng et al., 2026 ) , combines failed policy rollouts with action conditioning and failure-aware masking in a world-action model. However, it does not directly address how to repair released checkpoints while retaining their architecture and training objective, or which failure data are most effective under these constraints. To fill these knowledge gaps, we introduce CureWM , motivated by the observation that correctly predicting the outcome of an observed action does not imply knowing how a different action in the same context would change the outcome. CureWM perturbs successful demonstrations across a severity grid while preserving actions before intervention, verifies outcomes through execution, and retains failed and successful replays for post-training. The architecture and training objective remain unchanged. We evaluate four released checkpoints from two architecture families, which are Cosmos Policy ( Kim et al., 2026 ) and Ctrl-World ( Guo et al., 2026 ) , and test CureWM in simulation and on a physical robot arm. The ALOHA checkpoint is evaluated for diagnosis only (Appendix C ). Experiments on LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) and a physical robot show improved success–failure discrimination. Matched comparisons favor counterfactual failures over fresh policy failures, while ablations examine successful replays and verified outcome labels. These results also show why reduced optimism alone does not establish repair. Our contributions are as follows: 1. We introduce CureWM, which repairs released world models using execution-verified counterfactual replays without changing their architecture or training objective. 2. We demonstrate repair in simulation and on a physical robot, including improved success–failure discrimination and failure detection. Matched LIBERO comparisons show stronger discrimination than training on fresh policy failures. 3. We show that reduced optimism alone can overstate repair, and evaluate success–failure discrimination together with false alarms on successful actions.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: World models and action-conditioned reliability. Cosmos Policy ( Kim et al., 2026 ) predicts actions, future observations, and values for control and planning, while Ctrl-World ( Guo et al., 2026 ) supports policy evaluation and synthetic trajectory generation through action-conditioned video prediction. MiraBench ( Yang et al., 2026 ) evaluates physics adherence, action following, and optimism bias, and provides the perturbation families used in our experiments. WorldArena ( Shang et al., 2026 ) likewise distinguishes perceptual quality from functional utility. We study post-hoc repair. Our support argument relates to causal confusion in imitation learning ( de Haan et al., 2019 ) , but does not identify a causal mechanism inside the model. Failure and counterfactual supervision. Learning from unsuccessful behavior and constructed examples has been widely studied: Dex-Net ( Mahler et al., 2017 ) learns grasp robustness from synthetic examples with analytic labels, HER ( Andrychowicz et al., 2017 ) reuses unsuccessful attempts through goal relabeling, and CoDA ( Pitis et al., 2020 ) constructs counterfactual transitions using locally factored dynamics. AHA ( Duan et al., 2025 ) synthesizes manipulation failures to train a vision-language model for failure detection and natural-language reasoning. Concurrent FACT ( Peng et al., 2026 ) incorporates failed rollouts into world-action model training. We do not claim novelty in adding failure examples. CureWM combines controlled perturbations, execution-verified outcomes, and successful replay partners to repair released checkpoints with their original architecture and objective. Furthermore, matched comparisons test which data choices improve repair. Conservative values, failure detection, and predictive repair. Offline RL addresses unreliable extrapolation through data-constrained action selection ( Fujimoto et al., 2019 ) , conservative value learning ( Kumar et al., 2020 ) , and uncertainty-aware penalties or pessimistic dynamics ( Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . These methods motivate caution about unsupported actions, but conservative decision-making and accurate outcome discrimination are distinct objectives. Our label ablation illustrates that reduced optimism can accompany underestimated success predictions. It does not evaluate those offline RL algorithms. Foresight ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) instead learns failure detection from action-conditioned world-model representations. CureWM updates the world model’s own predictions. We assess whether it better distinguishes successful from failing actions, rather than simply assigning lower success values to both.

sections.heading: 3.1 Failure Insensitivity
sections.text: Let x t x_{t} denote the observation history and task context, and let a + t : T a^{+}_{t:T} and a − t : T a^{-}_{t:T} denote action sequences that succeed and fail from the same starting context. We call a model failure-insensitive when its predictions fail to distinguish these outcomes. Figure 1 illustrates this behavior. This differs from optimism alone: a model can assign similar values to successful and failing actions even when neither value is high. We therefore evaluate both predictions on failing actions and discrimination between successful and failing actions. Figure 1: Failure insensitivity on a held-out Franka counterfactual. From the same starting context, the original action sequence succeeds and a perturbed sequence fails under physical execution, yet the model predicts a success-like future for the failing sequence.

sections.heading: 3.3 CureWM
sections.text: CureWM constructs execution-verified action alternatives for post-training (Figure 2 ). It is motivated by the observation that, when only one action is observed per context, fitting its outcome does not require distinguishing the consequences of alternative actions. Proposition 1 in Appendix B formalizes this observation. Figure 2: The overview of CureWM. We perturb successful demonstrations at different severities, verify outcomes through execution, and use both successful and failing replays for post-training alongside the original training data. Severity values, outcome assignments, and predicted-value bars are used for illustration rather than measured results.

sections.heading: 4.1.1 Evaluation Setup
sections.text: The baseline and CureWM use official data from all four LIBERO suites; CureWM additionally uses counterfactual replays from LIBERO-Goal. Goal evaluation contains 484 verified failures and 1,196 successful perturbed replays from two independently generated sets using the training perturbation families and severity grid. Their source demonstrations are excluded from counterfactual construction but mostly present in the official data. The second set was generated after the compared models finished training. Spatial, Object, and LIBERO-10 test transfer without counterfactual training replays from those suites. Robot task success uses 500 episodes per suite and model.

The detailed numerical results are presented in Table 1 . On LIBERO-Goal, CureWM reduces value optimism from the baseline’s 79.55% to 30.17%, increases Δ SF \Delta_{\mathrm{SF}} from 0.003 to 0.282, and improves AUROC from 0.495 to 0.743. However, the proportion of successful replays incorrectly predicted to fail increases from 31.0% to 38.0%. CureWM improves discrimination, but the fixed-threshold detector predicts more successful replays as failures. Without counterfactual training replays from LIBERO-Spatial or LIBERO-Object, CureWM improves their AUROC from 0.522 and 0.466 to 0.629 and 0.587, respectively, alongside larger value gaps and lower optimism. On LIBERO-10, AUROC remains near chance at 0.493. At the fixed threshold of 0.5, low optimism of 2.51% coexists with a 99.4% false-positive rate. Thus, low optimism does not indicate reliable failure detection on this suite. Mean task success is 98.65% for Released, 96.80% for the baseline, and 96.55% for CureWM, whose changes relative to the baseline vary by suite (Table 1 ). Additional experiments assess training variability and discrimination within perturbation types. Across four independently fine-tuned CureWM models, Goal value optimism ranges from 30.2% to 43.0%, averaging 37.9% (Appendix D.2 ). Within 21 eligible perturbation-family–severity groups, mean AUROC increases from 0.537 to 0.714. The improvement therefore cannot be explained by perturbation type or severity alone (Appendix D.3 ). Experiments excluding individual perturbation types from counterfactual training show uneven transfer (Appendix D.4 ).

sections.text: We evaluate failure detection on 111 successful and 114 failing drawer and door manipulation rollouts excluded from training, reporting AUROC from predicted task-success values at 75% of episode length. Separately, we measure Δ SF \Delta_{\mathrm{SF}} on 120 examples with modified actions from official rollouts. These actions are not re-executed, so this evaluation measures prediction sensitivity rather than detection of verified failures. Robot task success is evaluated on OpenDrawer and CloseDoubleDoor from RoboCasa ( Nasiriany et al., 2024 ) over 30 episodes per task and model, using three evaluation seeds with ten episodes each.

sections.heading: 4.3.1 Evaluation Setup
sections.text: Starting from the same LIBERO-adapted Ctrl-World checkpoint, we compare CureWM with fine-tuning on unperturbed successful demonstrations. We evaluate predictions over four interaction steps (16 raw frames) using Equation 2 and frozen SVD ( Blattmann et al., 2023 ) VAE representations from three camera views. The evaluation contains 30 action pairs, including ten excluded from counterfactual training. The full set partially overlaps training.

sections.heading: 5.1 Evaluation Setup
sections.text: We evaluate CureWM on a Franka Research 3 using DROID-pretrained Ctrl-World ( Khazatsky et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) . Cup pick-and-place is the primary repair task. Cube picking tests task-specific repair and transfer from cup-task repair. Replay outcomes are verified through physical execution. After 1,400 steps of scene adaptation using successful demonstrations, we fine-tune CureWM on 90 failed replays, 24 successful wrist-tilt replays, and 31 unperturbed successful trajectories. The baseline uses only the same 31 unperturbed trajectories. Both receive 3,600 additional training steps, matching training duration but not distinct-data counts. Successful perturbed replays come only from wrist tilt and the other three tested perturbation types produce no successful replays at the evaluated severities. Data collection and splits are detailed in Appendix G.1 . Each of two hardware evaluations contains 15 failing action sequences paired with their original successful sequences from ten held-out demonstrations. These demonstrations and their perturbed replays are excluded from training. We measure visual optimism and success–failure discrimination using Equation 2 . We also measure failure-detection AUROC using distance to the image recorded at the end of each successful execution. Both diagnostics require recorded reference outcomes.

sections.heading: 6.2 Successful Replays from the Same Demonstrations
sections.text: The no-graded variant removes the 580 successful perturbed replays, while other-demo replaces them with successful replays from different demonstrations, approximately matched by perturbation family and severity. Both retain the 242 verified failures and original demonstration data. Across two independently fine-tuned models per variant, value optimism is 43.4–49.0% for no-graded and 44.8–60.1% for other-demo, compared with 30.2–43.0% across four full CureWM models. These results support an additional contribution from successful replays of the same demonstrations. However, the smallest observed difference is only 0.4 percentage points, and differences in task composition, sampling frequency, and training variation limit attribution to demonstration identity alone (Appendix D.5 ).

sections.heading: 6.3 Lower Optimism Does Not Always Mean Better Predictions
sections.text: Fresh policy failures reduce optimism by 12.4 percentage points while lowering values for both successful and failing actions (Table 5 ). Labeling all perturbed replays as failures, including 580 successful replays, also lowers training optimism but reduces the success-side value to 0.147. Its held-out value gap is 0.103 versus CureWM’s 0.282 (Appendix D.5 ). These comparisons motivate evaluating discrimination and fixed-threshold false-positive rates alongside optimism.

sections.heading: 6.4 Limitations
sections.text: Only 53 of 484 LIBERO-Goal failures come from demonstrations absent from the shared official data. Transfer across perturbation types and objects is inconsistent, and the prediction horizon limits observable failure consequences. Cosmos Policy’s video repair remains partial. Hardware evidence covers two objects on one robot, with small held-out samples and unequal training-data counts. CureWM requires executable counterfactual actions and verifiable outcomes; hardware detection also requires episode-specific references. Predictive gains do not establish improved control: RoboCasa exhibits a repair–control trade-off, best-of- N N selection shows no statistically established benefit, and policy ranking is untested.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduce CureWM, which repairs released robot world models using execution-verified counterfactual replays without changing their architecture or training objective. Experiments in simulation and on hardware show improved success–failure discrimination. Matched comparisons favor counterfactual failures over fresh policy failures at the tested budget, while ablations support retaining successful replays from the same demonstrations. These results also show why lower optimism alone does not establish repair. Broader transfer and improved robot control remain open challenges.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: We used generative AI (i.e., Claude and ChatGPT) tools to assist with drafting, revising, and polishing the manuscript, and to assist in proving the mathematical claims presented in Appendix B . The authors reviewed the AI-assisted text for accuracy and consistency with the experimental evidence. We also checked the mathematical arguments, including their assumptions, logical steps, and the scope of their conclusions, and revised them where necessary. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including all AI-assisted text, mathematical claims, and proofs.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: We provide anonymized code and analysis scripts in the supplementary materials. Section 3 describes counterfactual construction, execution-based outcome verification, and post-training. Appendix D.2 documents training settings, sampling configuration, and evaluated checkpoints. Data composition and evaluation splits are detailed in Appendices D.1 , E , F , and G.1 . Hardware evaluation, human assessment, and cube-task protocols are provided in Appendices G.2 , G.3 , and G.4 , respectively. The assumptions and proofs underlying our theoretical argument appear in Appendix B .

sections.heading: Appendix A Extended Related Work
sections.text: World models and their evaluation. Latent world models support learning through imagined interaction ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2025 ) , while video simulators extend prediction to visually rich environments ( Yang et al., 2024 ; NVIDIA, 2025a ; Guo et al., 2026 ) . Their potential use with generalist policies ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA, 2025b ) makes action-conditioned reliability important. MiraBench ( Yang et al., 2026 ) provides the perturbation families used in our experiments. Complementary evaluations examine embodied executability ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) and dynamic consistency ( Ruan et al., 2026 ) . Research on predictable world-model hallucinations connects diagnosis to data coverage and mitigation ( Hansen and Wang, 2026 ) . These works motivate evaluating consequences beyond visual plausibility. CureWM studies the response of released checkpoints to execution-verified counterfactual data. Failure data, detection, and recovery. Large manipulation datasets provide a broader data context ( Bu et al., 2025 ) . Failure judgments, detection, backup behavior, and counterfactual recovery are studied by AHA ( Duan et al., 2025 ) , Foresight ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) , AEGIS ( Chen, 2026 ) , and CoRe ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) . Counterfactual failure synthesis also supports recovery learning ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Our intervention changes the world model’s predictions through post-training. It is distinct from fitting a separate detector or selecting a recovery action, although these approaches can be complementary. Relation to FACT and negative-data learning. FACT ( Peng et al., 2026 ) combines failure data with world-action-model design and failure-aware masking. CureWM instead retains released architectures and their original objectives in its main treatment. Our matched fresh-failure experiment compares two data constructions within this fixed recipe and it is not an evaluation of FACT. More generally, learning from unsuccessful attempts, relabeled goals, and counterfactual augmentation has substantial work ( Mahler et al., 2017 ; Andrychowicz et al., 2017 ; Pitis et al., 2020 ) . Our contribution concerns the construction and evaluation of post-hoc repair data, not the introduction of negative examples. The support argument is also related to concerns about causal confusion ( de Haan et al., 2019 ) , without identifying a particular mechanism in the trained network. Conservative offline learning provides a separate context for distinguishing lower values from better discrimination ( Fujimoto et al., 2019 ; Kumar et al., 2020 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) .

sections.heading: B.4 Implications for CureWM
sections.text: The propositions motivate constructing action alternatives with execution-verified different outcomes under matched contexts. They do not establish that successful perturbed replays are necessary for repair: original demonstrations may already provide successful alternatives. Additional successful replays are evaluated empirically rather than justified by a necessity claim. Exact shared contexts are an idealization. A common source demonstration or action prefix does not by itself guarantee identical observed states during replay, especially on hardware. The argument also does not identify shared prefixes as the sole cause of the observed improvements, exclude useful learning from policy failures, or guarantee transfer to new tasks. Training-step comparisons at fixed data composition do not test the bound’s dependence on m / n m/n .

sections.heading: Appendix C Additional Diagnosis on ALOHA
sections.text: We evaluate the released Cosmos Policy checkpoint for ALOHA ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) on action sequences from 40 recorded episodes. For each episode, we apply three action edits: freezing the actions, reversing the action sequence, and opening both grippers. The reported changes in predicted task-success values are below 0.01 in magnitude, indicating limited sensitivity to these edits. The modified actions are not re-executed, so their outcomes are not verified. This experiment measures sensitivity to action changes, rather than prediction accuracy on confirmed failures. ALOHA is included for diagnosis only and we do not evaluate CureWM repair on this checkpoint.

sections.heading: D.1 Training Data and Evaluation Splits
sections.text: The official training data contain 2,000 records, including 300 failed policy rollouts. CureWM adds 822 counterfactual replay records: 242 verified failures and 580 successful replays. These include twelve repeated successful records. The failures comprise 23 approach-overshoot, seven carry-slip, 32 contact-oscillation, 56 insufficient-grip, 67 premature-release, and 57 wrist-tilt replays. Using one-based task and demonstration indices, counterfactual training uses demonstrations 1–3 per LIBERO-Goal task. The first evaluation set uses demonstrations 4–6, the second uses 7–9, and the other-demo comparison uses demonstrations 10–12. Sources whose original action sequence fails during replay are skipped, leaving 27 training sources and 56 evaluation sources. The second evaluation set is generated after the compared models finish training. The evaluation contains 484 failures from 45 source demonstrations and 1,196 successful perturbed replays. All compared models use the same evaluation records. The training-pool evaluations instead use two groups containing 115 and 127 failures. These are in-sample for CureWM and do not establish held-out repair. Most evaluation demonstrations also occur in the shared official training data. Three are absent: task 4/demonstration 6, task 7/demonstration 5, and task 4/demonstration 9. They contribute 20, 12, and 21 failures, respectively. On these 53 failures, value optimism is 26.4%, 28.3%, and 11.3% for the released model, baseline, and CureWM. With only three source demonstrations, this subset does not isolate demonstration familiarity from task and failure-type differences. The LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, and LIBERO-10 evaluations contain 367/443, 286/524, and 359/331 failed/successful perturbed replays, respectively. Their official data remain included in fine-tuning, but their counterfactual replays do not enter training. The suite means in Table 1 weight the four suites equally.

Successful and failing trajectories are sampled through the existing training procedure, not supplied as explicit positive–negative pairs. Training-record counts therefore do not directly specify sampling probabilities. LIBERO uses batch size 4 and a default learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} . sections.heading: Fresh policy failures.
sections.text: We execute the released policy with stochastic sampling for 16 passes over ten LIBERO-Goal tasks and 50 initial states per task, totaling 8,000 episodes. The collection yields 238 verified failures. 61.8% occur on two tasks, while one task has no observed failure. Zero observed failures does not imply zero failure probability. For each task, we take the smaller of the available policy-failure and counterfactual-failure counts. This gives 140 distinct failures per source. Each set is repeated to form 242 training records and combined with the same 580 successful counterfactual replays and 2,000 official records. Both models train for 7,500 steps. Thus distinct-failure counts, per-task counts, training-record counts, successful replay data, and training duration are matched. Of the 140 selected policy failures, 69 have a recorded success from the same task and initial-state index. None shares an exactly identical first executed action with its successful counterpart. This criterion requires numerical equality of every action component but it does not test approximate action similarity. All collected policy failures reach the 300-step limit, which does not identify when a failure-causing event occurred. These construction differences do not establish a unique explanation for the matched comparison in Table 5 .

sections.heading: Existing policy failures.
sections.text: The own-failure comparison repeatedly samples 300 failures already present in the official mixture to produce 822 additional training records. Unlike the fresh comparison, it does not match task coverage, novelty, or repetition. It therefore tests this specific reuse of existing failures rather than policy-failure learning in general.

sections.heading: Successful replay partners.
sections.text: No-graded removes the 580 successful replay records. Other-demo replaces them with 580 verified successes from demonstrations 10–12 per task, approximately matched by perturbation type and severity. These comparisons change training-data composition; record counts alone do not guarantee equal exposure under the sampling procedure.

sections.heading: Outcome verification.
sections.text: The unverified-label comparison assigns failure labels to all perturbed replays, including the 580 successful records, while retaining the remaining training procedure. It achieves 57.9% held-out optimism and a value gap of 0.103, compared with CureWM’s 30.2% and 0.282. On training failures, its optimism is 10.3%, below CureWM’s 16.9%. However, its mean value for successful actions is only 0.147 and its value gap is 0.062. Lower training optimism therefore overstates repair: the model also lowers successful-action predictions.

sections.heading: Failed-action supervision.
sections.text: Masking only action-prediction loss on failed LIBERO replays gives 32.9% held-out optimism and a value gap of 0.258, compared with 30.2% and 0.282 without masking. Substantial value-side repair remains without supervising those failed actions. This prediction comparison does not establish a closed-loop benefit from masking.

sections.heading: D.6 Value and Video Predictions
sections.text: Cosmos Policy’s value and video predictions do not improve equally. On the first held-out set of 231 failures, value optimism is 71.4%, 72.7%, and 28.1% for the released model, baseline, and CureWM, while visual optimism is 58.0%, 55.8%, and 45.0%. The results support partial video repair, rather than uniform improvement across prediction outputs.

Across four released checkpoints from two architecture families, we observe weak sensitivity to action changes and success-like predictions on verified failures. Although recent work incorporates failures into model training, which data can repair released checkpoints without changing their architecture or training objective still remains underexplored. To this end, we introduce CureWM , which constructs alternative actions from successful demonstrations across a severity grid, verifies their outcomes through execution in simulation or on hardware, and fine-tunes released models on the resulting failures and surviving successes alongside nominal demonstrations. This construction provides controlled action contrasts from shared starting contexts. On 484 held-out LIBERO failure counterfactuals, optimism falls from 80% after fine-tuning on the official data to 30–43% across four independently fine-tuned CureWM models (38% mean). In two separate evaluations on a physical robot arm, failure predictions scored as success-like by a latent-distance diagnostic decrease from 90% after fine-tuning on successful demonstrations alone to 33% with CureWM. With failure counts per task, successful replay data, and training budget matched, counterfactual failures yield a success–failure value gap of 0.124, compared with 0.014 for freshly collected on-policy failures. These findings support execution-verified counterfactual replay for post-hoc repair and show why reduced optimism must be evaluated alongside success–failure discrimination. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/CureWM . 1 Introduction Robot world models learn to predict how environments evolve in response to actions, from latent dynamics models to generative video simulators ( Hafner et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; NVIDIA, 2025a ) . In the robotic domain, their predictions support policy evaluation in imagination ( Guo et al., 2026 ) , action selection and planning ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , and synthetic experience generation for policy learning ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) . These applications require more than visually plausible futures: a model must distinguish actions that accomplish the task from those that fail. If failing actions receive high success values or generate success-like futures, decisions based on these predictions can favor actions that do not achieve the intended outcome. However, how to repair failure prediction in released robot world models still remains underexplored. MiraBench ( Yang et al., 2026 ) found optimism bias in action-conditioned predictions, but diagnosing such failure insensitivity does not tell us which training data could correct it. In particular, failed trajectories need not teach a model how alternative actions from the same context change the outcome. This distinction matters for released checkpoints: simply adding failures may lower predicted success across both successful and failing actions, reducing the optimism without improving discrimination. Therefore, the question is which kind of data enable post-hoc repair of action-conditioned predictions, and how to distinguish that repair from a general shift toward pessimism. Concurrent work, such as FACT ( Peng et al., 2026 ) , combines failed policy rollouts with action conditioning and failure-aware masking in a world-action model. However, it does not directly address how to repair released checkpoints while retaining their architecture and training objective, or which failure data are most effective under these constraints. To fill these knowledge gaps, we introduce CureWM , motivated by the observation that correctly predicting the outcome of an observed action does not imply knowing how a different action in the same context would change the outcome. CureWM perturbs successful demonstrations across a severity grid while preserving actions before intervention, verifies outcomes through execution, and retains failed and successful replays for post-training. The architecture and training objective remain unchanged. We evaluate four released checkpoints from two architecture families, which are Cosmos Policy ( Kim et al., 2026 ) and Ctrl-World ( Guo et al., 2026 ) , and test CureWM in simulation and on a physical robot arm. The ALOHA checkpoint is evaluated for diagnosis only (Appendix C ). Experiments on LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) and a physical robot show improved success–failure discrimination. Matched comparisons favor counterfactual failures over fresh policy failures, while ablations examine successful replays and verified outcome labels. These results also show why reduced optimism alone does not establish repair. Our contributions are as follows: 1. We introduce CureWM, which repairs released world models using execution-verified counterfactual replays without changing their architecture or training objective. 2. We demonstrate repair in simulation and on a physical robot, including improved success–failure discrimination and failure detection. Matched LIBERO comparisons show stronger discrimination than training on fresh policy failures. 3. We show that reduced optimism alone can overstate repair, and evaluate success–failure discrimination together with false alarms on successful actions. 2 Related Work World models and action-conditioned reliability. Cosmos Policy ( Kim et al., 2026 ) predicts actions, future observations, and values for control and planning, while Ctrl-World ( Guo et al., 2026 ) supports policy evaluation and synthetic trajectory generation through action-conditioned video prediction. MiraBench ( Yang et al., 2026 ) evaluates physics adherence, action following, and optimism bias, and provides the perturbation families used in our experiments. WorldArena ( Shang et al., 2026 ) likewise distinguishes perceptual quality from functional utility. We study post-hoc repair. Our support argument relates to causal confusion in imitation learning ( de Haan et al., 2019 ) , but does not identify a causal mechanism inside the model. Failure and counterfactual supervision. Learning from unsuccessful behavior and constructed examples has been widely studied: Dex-Net ( Mahler et al., 2017 ) learns grasp robustness from synthetic examples with analytic labels, HER ( Andrychowicz et al., 2017 ) reuses unsuccessful attempts through goal relabeling, and CoDA ( Pitis et al., 2020 ) constructs counterfactual transitions using locally factored dynamics. AHA ( Duan et al., 2025 ) synthesizes manipulation failures to train a vision-language model for failure detection and natural-language reasoning. Concurrent FACT ( Peng et al., 2026 ) incorporates failed rollouts into world-action model training. We do not claim novelty in adding failure examples. CureWM combines controlled perturbations, execution-verified outcomes, and successful replay partners to repair released checkpoints with their original architecture and objective. Furthermore, matched comparisons test which data choices improve repair. Conservative values, failure detection, and predictive repair. Offline RL addresses unreliable extrapolation through data-constrained action selection ( Fujimoto et al., 2019 ) , conservative value learning ( Kumar et al., 2020 ) , and uncertainty-aware penalties or pessimistic dynamics ( Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) . These methods motivate caution about unsupported actions, but conservative decision-making and accurate outcome discrimination are distinct objectives. Our label ablation illustrates that reduced optimism can accompany underestimated success predictions. It does not evaluate those offline RL algorithms. Foresight ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) instead learns failure detection from action-conditioned world-model representations. CureWM updates the world model’s own predictions. We assess whether it better distinguishes successful from failing actions, rather than simply assigning lower success values to both. 3 Method 3.1 Failure Insensitivity Let x t x_{t} denote the observation history and task context, and let a + t : T a^{+}_{t:T} and a − t : T a^{-}_{t:T} denote action sequences that succeed and fail from the same starting context. Transfer across perturbation types and objects is inconsistent, and the prediction horizon limits observable failure consequences. Cosmos Policy’s video repair remains partial. Hardware evidence covers two objects on one robot, with small held-out samples and unequal training-data counts. CureWM requires executable counterfactual actions and verifiable outcomes; hardware detection also requires episode-specific references. Predictive gains do not establish improved control: RoboCasa exhibits a repair–control trade-off, best-of- N N selection shows no statistically established benefit, and policy ranking is untested. 7 Conclusion We introduce CureWM, which repairs released robot world models using execution-verified counterfactual replays without changing their architecture or training objective. Experiments in simulation and on hardware show improved success–failure discrimination. Matched comparisons favor counterfactual failures over fresh policy failures at the tested budget, while ablations support retaining successful replays from the same demonstrations. These results also show why lower optimism alone does not establish repair. Broader transfer and improved robot control remain open challenges.
